καιρὸν ὄντα ἐν ἡμέραις πονηραῖς οἱονεὶ μεταποιοῦμεν τὰς πονηρὰς ἡμέρας εἰς
ἀγαθάς, καὶ ὡσπερεὶ ἑαυτοῖς ποιοῦμεν αὐτὰς εἶναι οὐ τοῦ ἐνε τῶτο αἰῶνο ἡμέρας
πονηρὰ ἀλλὰ τοῦ μέλλοντο αἰῶνο ἡμέρας ἀγαθάς. 〚[v. 17] διὰ τοῦτο μὴ γίνεσθε
ἄφρονες ἀλλὰ συνιέντες τί τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Κυρίου. διὰ ποῖον τοῦτο, ἢ τὸ βλέπειν
ἀκριβῶς πῶς περιπατεῖτε μὴ ὡς ἄσοφοι ἀλλ' ὡς σοφοί, μὴ γίνεσθε ἄφρονες; εἰ γὰρ
ἔσεσθε ἄφρονες, ἀκριβῶς οὐ περιπατή σετε οὐδὲ ὡς σοφοί. προστάσσει δὲ αὐτοῖς τὸ
τοῦ Κυρίου ἐξετάζειν θέλημα καὶ συνιέναι αὐτό, ἵν' ὅπου τι περὶ τοῦ πράττειν
καταλάβοιεν, αὐτὸ πράττωσιν ὡς θέλημα Κυρίου, ὅπου δὲ πάσχ<ω>σι φέρ<ω>σιν
αὐτὸ ὡς θελήματι γινόμενον Κυρίου.〛 28 Eph. v18 καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ ἐν ᾧ
ἐστὶν ἀσωτία, ἀλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι. [Ὠριγένης φησί] δύναται μὲν καὶ
ἁπλούστερον ταῦτα νοεῖσθαι, ἀσωτίας οὔσης ἐν τῇ χρήσει τοῦ μεθύειν ποιοῦντος
οἴνου. δύναται δὲ καὶ οἶνος ἐν ᾧ ἐστὶν ἀσωτία νοεῖσθαι περὶ οὗ ἐν ᾠδῇ μεγάλῃ
λέγεται θυμὸ δρακόντων ὁ οἶνο αὐτῶν καὶ θυμὸ ἀ πίδων ἀνίατο , ὅντινα πάντες οἱ
ἐξιστάμενοι καὶ μεθύοντες τὸν λογισμὸν πίνουσι πολλὴν ἔχοντα τὴν ἀσωτίαν. πρὸς
ἀντιδιαστολὴν δὲ ἐκείνου τοῦ οἴνου τοῦ μεθύσκοντος ἐν ᾧ ἐστὶν ἀσωτία ἐναντίος
νοεῖται ὁ πεπληρωμένος πνεύματι καὶ πᾶν ὃ χωρεῖ τοῦ θειοτέρου λαμβάνων.
πολλάκις δὲ τετηρήκαμεν τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ «πνεύματος» χωρὶς προσθήκης γεγραμμένον
ὅτι ἐπὶ κρείττονος εἴρηται, ὅπερ καὶ ἐνθάδε σημαίνεται. 29 Eph. v19 [λαλοῦντες
ἑαυτοῖς ψαλμοῖς καὶ ὕμνοις καὶ ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς, ᾄδοντες καὶ ψάλλοντες ἐν τῇ
καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν τῷ Κυρίῳ.] [Ὠριγένης δέ φησιν] οἱ μὲν ὕμνοι δύναμιν καὶ θειότητα
καταγγέλλουσι τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ εἴη ἂν ὁ ἐπιστήμων τοῦ θεολογεῖν ἐν ὕμνοις
πνευματικοῖς· τάχα δὲ ὁ περὶ τῶν πρακτέων διαλαμβάνων καὶ τῶν οἷς δεῖ ἐνεργεῖν
διὰ τοῦ ὡς ψαλτηρίου ὀργάνου σωματικοῦ ἡμῶν, οὗτος ἐν ψαλμοῖς ἐστι
πνευματικοῖς· ὁ δὲ ἄλλως φυσιολογῶν περὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου τάξεως καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν
δημιουργημάτων, οὗτος ἐν ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς. καὶ χρή γε ᾄδειν κατὰ τὴν
φυσιολογίαν καὶ ψάλλειν κατὰ τὴν περὶ τῶν ἠθῶν διέξοδον τῷ Κυρίῳ διακείμενον
γνησίως πρὸς τὰ λεγόμενα· τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι τὸ ψάλλειν καὶ ᾄδειν τῇ καρδίᾳ τῷ
Κυρίῳ. [v 20] εὐχαριστοῦντες πάντοτε ὑπὲρ πάντων ἐν ὀνόματι τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν
Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τῷ Θεῷ καὶ πατρί. καὶ ἐν τῇ πρὸς Θεσσαλονικεῖς προτέρᾳ φησί
πάντοτε χαίρετε ἀδιαλείπτω προ εύχε θε ἐν παντὶ εὐχαρι τεῖτε. ταύτην δὴ τηρήσει
τὴν ἐντολὴν ὁ διειληφὼς περὶ τῆς προνοίας φθανούσης καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ βʹ ἀ αρίων
πωλούμενα πέντε τρουθία ὧν ἓν οὐ πίπτει εἰ παγίδα χωρὶ τοῦ ἐν οὐρανοῖ πατρό .
τὸ δὲ ἐν παντὶ εὐχαριστεῖν καὶ ὑπὲρ πάντων εὐχαριστεῖν ἐστιν· οὐκοῦν καὶ ἐπὶ ταῖς

καταθεᾶσθαι τὸ κάλλος αὐτοῦ καὶ θεωρεῖν ὅσα καὶ οἷα γέγονε διὰ τὸ λογικόν, οὕτως
καὶ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐν μέρει εὐχαριστητέον. τὸν δὲ εὐχαριστοῦντα τῷ Θεῷ καὶ πατρὶ ἐν τῷ
με ίτῃ Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων εὐχαριστεῖν χρή, ὥστε ἡμᾶς ποιῆσαι τὸ ἐν ὀνόματι τοῦ

pass_a_gloss: ... needed and on the acquisition of the blessed life spending it. And buying out the season which is in wicked days we as it were transform the wicked days into good, and as it were make them be for ourselves not wicked days of the present age but good days of the coming age. Eph 5:17 (in double brackets in the edition): on account of this do not become senseless but understanding what the will of the Lord is. On account of what is this; or is it, on account of seeing precisely how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, do not become senseless? For if you will be senseless, you will not walk precisely nor as wise. And he orders them to examine the will of the Lord and to understand it, so that where they grasp something about the acting they may do it as will of the Lord, and where they suffer they may bear it as happening by will of the Lord. Eph 5:18: and do not be made drunk with wine in which is profligacy, but be filled in spirit. [Origen says] These things can be understood also more simply, there being profligacy in the use of the wine that makes drunk. But the wine in which is profligacy can also be understood about that of which in the great ode it is said "the wine of them is fury of dragons and incurable fury of asps", which all who are out of themselves and drunk in reasoning drink, having much profligacy. And for contrast with that wine that makes drunk in which is profligacy, the opposite is understood: the one having been filled with spirit and receiving everything of the more divine that he has room for. And often we have observed the name of the spirit written without addition being said upon the better, which is signified here also. Eph 5:19 lemma: speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and odes spiritual, singing and psalming in your heart to the Lord. [Origen says] The hymns announce power and divinity of God, and the one knowing how to theologize would be in spiritual hymns; but perhaps the one discussing about the things to be done and those which one must work through our bodily organ as through a psaltery, this one is in spiritual psalms; and the one otherwise discoursing on nature about the order of the cosmos and the remaining works of craftsmanship, this one is in spiritual odes. And it is needed to sing according to the natural study and to psalm according to the going-through of the moral characters to the Lord, being genuinely disposed toward the things said; for this is the psalming and singing in the heart to the Lord. Eph 5:20: giving thanks always over all things in name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and Father. Also in the former letter to the Thessalonians he says "rejoice always, pray unceasingly, in everything give thanks". This command indeed will keep the one who has understood about the providence reaching even upon the five sparrows sold for two assaria, of which one does not fall into a trap apart from the Father in the heavens. But giving thanks in everything is also giving thanks over all things; therefore also over the circumstances one must give thanks, since these too are among the things over which one must give thanks; and as the one in the world must give thanks in partaking of the world and beholding its beauty and contemplating how many and of what sort things came to be because of the rational, so also over the things in part one must give thanks. And the one giving thanks to God and Father must give thanks in the mediator of God and men, so that we do the "in name of our Lord Jesus Christ give thanks to God and Father". Eph 5:21: being subjected, he says, to one another in fear of Christ. This is quite destructive of being lover of rule and lover of first place. For to all this command has been given: for being free from all I enslaved myself to all, that I might gain all. But also the command saying "serve as slaves one another" orders this. Wherefore through love the apostles slaved for the churches, doing service and ministering to the salvation of men. And the Savior himself took up the form of a slave not so much on account of something else as on account of having slaved for the disciples, so that also having once put water into the basin he washed the feet of the disciples. But also the one who has understood "the one wishing to be great among you will be slave of all" is subjected according to slaving for whom one must. It is possible however for the one slaving, doing in the slaving the things fitting to those slaved for, to seem not to be subjected, when through not knowing the beneficial things those slaved for command those wishing to slave to do things not suitable to them. But even then the one doing toward the benefit both slaves and is subjected to the need of the one for whom he slaves, on account of the passionless and blessed-making fear according to the word of God. For this I suppose ...
pass_b_english: needful and on gaining the blessed life. And when we redeem the time that lies in evil days, we change the evil days, as it were, into good ones; for ourselves we make them, as it were, not evil days of the present age but good days of the age to come.

"Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is" (Ephesians 5:17). "Therefore": because of what? Is it that, because you are to look carefully how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, you must not become foolish? For if you are foolish, you will not walk carefully, nor as the wise do. He commands them to search out the will of the Lord and to understand it, so that wherever they grasp something about what they should do, they may do it as the Lord's will, and wherever they suffer, they may bear it as something that happens by the Lord's will.

"And do not get drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled in spirit" (Ephesians 5:18). Origen says: These words can be understood quite simply, since debauchery lies in drinking the wine that makes one drunk. But "wine, in which is debauchery," can also be understood of the wine spoken of in the great Song: "Their wine is the rage of dragons, and the incurable rage of asps" (Deuteronomy 32:33). All who are out of their minds and drunk in their reasoning drink this wine, and it is full of debauchery. Set against that wine, which makes drunk and in which is debauchery, is its opposite: the one who has been filled with spirit and receives all of what is more divine that he has room for. We have often observed that the word "spirit," written without any addition, is said of the better; and that is what it means here too.

"Speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord" (Ephesians 5:19). Origen says: Hymns proclaim the power and divinity of God, and the one who has knowledge of how to speak of God would be in spiritual hymns. Perhaps the one who treats of what is to be done, and of the things one must carry out through our body as through an instrument, a kind of psaltery, is in spiritual psalms; and the one who, on the other hand, studies nature, the order of the world and the rest of what was made, is in spiritual songs. And we must sing in keeping with the study of nature, and make melody in keeping with the account of conduct, to the Lord, sincerely disposed toward what is said; for this is what it is to make melody and sing in the heart to the Lord.

"Always giving thanks for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father" (Ephesians 5:20). In the First Letter to the Thessalonians, too, he says, "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything" (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18). This commandment will be kept by the one who has understood that providence reaches even to the five sparrows sold for two pennies, not one of which falls into a snare without the Father in heaven. To give thanks in everything is also to give thanks for everything. So we must give thanks for hardships too, since these are also among the things for which we must give thanks. And just as a person in the world must give thanks for sharing in the world, for gazing at its beauty, and for seeing how many and what kind of things have come to be for the sake of the rational creature, so too we must give thanks for particular things. Whoever gives thanks to God and the Father must give thanks in the mediator between God and humankind, so that we do what is written: give thanks in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father.

"Submitting," he says, "to one another in the fear of Christ" (Ephesians 5:21). This tears down entirely the love of ruling and of being first. For this commandment is given to all: "For though I am free from all, I made myself a slave to all, that I might win all" (1 Corinthians 9:19). And the commandment that says, "Serve one another," orders the same (Galatians 5:13). That is why the apostles, through love, served the churches as slaves, ministering and serving the salvation of human beings. The Savior himself took the form of a slave, not so much for any other reason as to serve his disciples as a slave, so that once he even poured water into the basin and washed the disciples' feet (John 13:5). And the one who has understood, "Whoever wishes to be great among you shall be the slave of all," submits by serving those whom he ought.

It is possible, however, for one who serves, and who in his service does what is suited to those he serves, to seem not to submit. This happens when those being served, not knowing what is good for them, order those who want to serve them to do things that are not suited to them. Yet even then the one who acts for their good both serves and submits to the need of the one he serves, because of the fear that, according to the word of God, is free of passion and makes us blessed. choices.why: The edition sets the Eph 5:17 comment in double brackets; it is kept in the reading text with no apparatus, and the brackets are recorded in source_note.
Origen's comment reads πνεῦμα without article and argues that 'spirit' without addition means the better part; lower-case keeps his reading open.
Origen assigns hymns to speaking of God, psalms to conduct carried out through the body (the psaltery), songs to the study of nature; the English keeps the three apart.
The section ends inside the sentence; u06-rem-close begins with δηλοῦσθαι ἐκ τοῦ ἐν φόβῳ Χριστοῦ.
